mcqs.question: A table sharded by range on an auto-incrementing order ID sees all new writes hit the single shard holding the highest ID range, while older shards sit nearly idle. What's the underlying cause?
options: The shard key is monotonically increasing, so every new write falls into the same, newest range
The database's replication is misconfigured
The table has too many indexes
Range partitioning always distributes writes evenly regardless of key pattern
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic range-partitioning failure mode: a monotonic key means every new row's value is the highest seen so far, so it always lands in the newest range on one shard. It's unrelated to replication or indexing, and range partitioning explicitly does not guarantee even distribution for skewed key patterns.

mcqs.question: A time-series metrics table is almost always queried as "give me all readings for sensor X between timestamp A and B." Which partitioning scheme fits best, and why?
options: Hash partitioning, because it always distributes load more evenly than range partitioning
Range partitioning, because the dominant query pattern is a contiguous range that a range scheme can serve from one or few shards
Neither scheme works for time-series data
It doesn't matter, since both schemes perform identically for range queries
mcqs.explanation: Range partitioning keeps genuinely range-queried workloads fast by keeping contiguous keys together on the same shard(s). Hash partitioning would scatter this exact range across every shard, forcing a fan-out for a query that should be cheap. The two schemes are not interchangeable for range-heavy access patterns.

mcqs.question: Why does adding one shard to a cluster using plain `hash(key) mod N` force a near-total data reshuffle, while consistent hashing only moves roughly 1/N of the data?
options: Because plain mod-N hashing is a slower algorithm than consistent hashing
Because consistent hashing doesn't actually store any data, only metadata
Because changing N changes the mod result for almost every key, while consistent hashing's ring only reassigns the keys between the new shard and its neighbor
Because plain mod-N hashing only works with exactly 2 shards
mcqs.explanation: With mod-N, changing N shifts the modulo result for nearly every key, forcing almost all data to move. Consistent hashing avoids this because a new shard only claims the portion of the ring between itself and its neighbor, moving a small, bounded fraction of keys. Speed of the hash function and shard count aren't the relevant factors here.

mcqs.question: A multi-tenant system shards by `tenant_id`. One enterprise customer is 200x larger than a typical tenant and its shard is consistently overloaded, even though the hash function distributes tenant IDs perfectly evenly. What does this indicate?
options: The hash function must be broken since it should have caught this
The overloaded shard needs more replicas to fix the problem
Sharding by tenant_id is always the wrong choice for any multi-tenant system
This is a hot partition caused by real-world access-pattern skew, not key-distribution skew, and a uniform hash can't fix it
mcqs.explanation: A perfectly even hash only guarantees even key distribution, not even real-world load — one outsized tenant on its own shard is a hot partition regardless. Sharding by tenant_id isn't always wrong (it gives clean isolation), and adding replicas addresses read scale, not the write/storage imbalance this describes.

mcqs.question: A payments system needs to atomically debit one account and credit another, but the two accounts happen to hash to different shards. What does this situation call for?
options: A normal single-node database transaction works fine across shards with no changes
This is impossible to solve and the accounts must be merged onto one shard permanently
A distributed transaction protocol (e.g. two-phase commit), or a shard-key redesign so both accounts co-locate on the same shard
Sharding should be abandoned entirely for financial data
mcqs.explanation: Cross-shard atomicity genuinely needs either a distributed transaction protocol or a design change that co-locates the related rows on one shard — a plain single-node transaction can't span two independent shards. It's solvable, doesn't require abandoning sharding altogether, and permanent merging isn't the only option.

mcqs.question: What is the core engineering challenge in resharding a live production system, beyond picking a new hashing scheme?
options: Safely migrating and verifying data consistency across the old and new layouts while the system stays live — the migration and verification problem, not the hashing algorithm
Choosing a faster programming language for the migration script
There is no additional challenge once a new hashing scheme is chosen
Resharding always requires taking the system offline, so there's nothing more to plan
mcqs.explanation: The hard part of live resharding is the dual-write/backfill/verify/cutover process that keeps data correct and available throughout — the hashing scheme itself is comparatively simple. Downtime isn't required with modern approaches, and there is real additional work beyond picking an algorithm.
